section1_theory.title: A visitor, not yet an analyst
section1_theory.subtitle: Welcome to CDAC Bengaluru & The First Golden Rule of SOC Triage
section1_theory.content:
Welcome to the fictionalised CDAC Bengaluru Security Operations Centre (SOC) learning environment. As you step through the reception doors, morning light falls across the training campus, and you receive an orientation badge reading “SOC Learner.”

Mentor Ananya, the SOC shift lead, greets you warmly:
“Welcome. You do not need an IT background, and nobody expects you to investigate an attack today.”
You might reply: “I use a phone and a laptop every day, but I do not understand what happens inside them.”
Ananya smiles: “That is our exact starting point. First, we will understand ordinary activity; later, we will recognise activity that needs checking.”

The Cardinal Rule of Security Operations
In security monitoring, beginners often fear that they will make a mistake or feel pressured to click buttons hastily when an alert sounds. Ananya establishes our foundational rule right away:
“First question: if a screen shows something unfamiliar, should you guess, change it, or ask for help?”
The only safe and professional response is:
“Ask for help before changing anything.”
Ananya confirms: “Exactly. Curiosity is welcome; unsupported action is not.”

Why Ordinary Activity Comes First
You cannot spot an anomaly without knowing what normal looks like. In cybersecurity, defenders call this the "operational baseline." Before opening complex security consoles, we first learn how an everyday computer boots up, how files are stored, and how people communicate across networks. When you encounter something strange, disciplined analysts do not guess—they observe, record, and verify.
section1_theory.keyTakeaway: Curiosity is welcome; unsupported action is not. Never guess when encountering unfamiliar activity—always observe and ask for help before changing anything.

section1_theory.title: The centre and its people
section1_theory.subtitle: The 6 Teaching Zones & Why the SOC Does Not Own Every Service
section1_theory.content:
Mentor Ananya brings up an illustrated map of the CDAC Bengaluru learning facility. The map highlights six distinct teaching zones:
1. Staff Support (Hardware, peripherals, desktop setups)
2. Computing & Workstations (End-user devices and operating systems)
3. Network Services (Switches, routers, firewalls, and campus cabling)
4. Identity Services (User accounts, passwords, MFA credentials, permissions)
5. Security Monitoring (The SOC: telemetry streams, alert queues, triage)
6. Response Coordination (Playbooks, incident containment, recovery)
(Alongside an Industrial Demonstration Zone simulating factory PLCs).

Ananya clarifies immediately:
“These are teaching zones, not a claim about the real organisation's departments or infrastructure.”
The learner asks an essential question:
“Does the SOC repair every computer and run every department?”
Ananya responds firmly:
“No. It monitors security and coordinates with people who own devices, accounts, networks, and business services.”

Why Boundaries and Cooperation Matter
A common misconception among beginners is that cybersecurity analysts control every computer, rewrite every application, and replace broken hardware. In reality, modern enterprises rely on specialized division of responsibility:
- If an employee spills tea on their keyboard, they contact Staff Support.
- If a staff member forgets their domain password, Identity Services manages credential resets.
- If a network cable is unplugged, Network Services investigates the switch port.
- When an anomalous after-hours sign-in alert fires, the Security Monitoring team investigates.

Ananya poses the key question:
“Who should investigate an alert while keeping the service owner informed?”
The learner replies:
“The security team, with the appropriate owner's help.”
Ananya smiles:
“Correct. Cooperation matters more than pretending one team knows everything.”
section1_theory.keyTakeaway: The SOC monitors security and coordinates with service owners—it does not own or repair every system in the enterprise. Cooperation matters more than pretending one team knows everything.

formalDefinitions.definition: The individual or business unit accountable for the delivery, maintenance, and operational integrity of a specific IT service or system.

terminologyScaffolding.definition: The organizational division of responsibilities where the Security Operations Centre (SOC) monitors threats and coordinates responses, while distinct IT and business teams own and maintain devices, accounts, networks, and services.
terminologyScaffolding.whyItMatters: Eliminates the dangerous misconception that the SOC runs every department or fixes every broken keyboard; effective security depends on close cooperation with service owners.

section1_theory.title: Your practice space
section1_theory.subtitle: The Blue-Bordered Console, Virtual Machine Isolation & Lab Scope
section1_theory.content:
Mentor Ravi steps forward to introduce your practice workstation. As you look at the monitor, a distinct blue border surrounds the desktop. Nearby, an illustration of a locked heavy doorway represents production enterprise operations.

Ravi explains the safety boundary:
“Everything you touch in this course is a supplied simulation, training dataset, or explicitly authorised isolated lab.”
The learner asks a natural question:
“Can a virtual machine affect something outside the lab?”
Ravi answers directly:
“Yes, if configured badly. Use the supplied isolation settings; a virtual machine is not automatically a safety barrier.”

How Virtual Machines Work & Why Isolation Matters
A Virtual Machine (VM) is a software computer running inside physical hardware. It feels like an independent PC, with its own operating system and files. However, if a virtual machine is set to "Bridged" network mode, it shares the physical network card with the host computer—meaning any scan, payload, or network traffic can reach production servers, campus Wi-Fi, or home routers!

To prevent accidental leaks, our training environment enforces two strict safeguards:
1. Host-Only Network Isolation: The VM communicates only with simulated training nodes inside your console. All outbound internet and local network bridging are disabled.
2. Snapshot Rollback: Before testing any command or opening a practice sample, the system records a clean snapshot. If anything breaks, a single reset restores the clean baseline in seconds.

The Lab Boundary Rule
Ravi tests your understanding:
“May you point a lab exercise at your college network without permission?”
The learner replies:
“No. Permission for this lab does not include other systems.”
Ravi confirms:
“Correct. Stop and ask whenever the lab boundary is unclear.”
section1_theory.keyTakeaway: A virtual machine is not automatically a safety barrier—always use supplied isolation settings. Practice stays strictly within authorized boundaries; never point lab tools at outside or production networks.
section1_theory.cdacScenario: Mentor Ravi demonstrates sandbox networking, snapshot resets, and the strict rules governing lab boundaries.

formalDefinitions.definition: A controlled, segregated compute environment configured to prevent software execution or network communications from impacting production systems.

questions.question: Is a virtual machine (VM) automatically a guaranteed safety barrier on its own?

Yes, because virtual machines do not use electricity
No, virtual machines cannot run software
questions.explanation: As Mentor Ravi warns, a VM is not automatically safe on its own. Misconfigured network adapters can expose outside networks unless host-only isolation is active.

section1_theory.title: A clue worth preserving
section1_theory.subtitle: Evidence Integrity, Working Copies & The Power of a Safe Pause
section1_theory.content:
Mentor Ananya brings up two files side-by-side on your console screen. On the left is an original raw log file named auth_raw.log. On the right is a second file named auth_working_copy.log.

Ananya defines digital evidence:
“Evidence is information another analyst can inspect, not just your memory of what happened.”
The learner notices messy, unformatted lines in the original file and asks:
“Can I tidy the original file so it looks clearer?”
Ananya responds with an immediate, vital lesson:
“Keep the original intact. Work on a copy and record its source, collection time, and your actions.”

The Evidentiary Chain & Why Originals Are Untouchable
In cybersecurity investigations, an alert may eventually lead to a formal incident report, human resources action, or even legal proceedings. If an analyst modifies, reformats, or deletes lines from an original log file—even with the best intentions—the integrity of the entire investigation is permanently destroyed!
To preserve evidence integrity, analysts follow three golden habits:
1. Make the Original Read-Only: Never edit the source file. Compute its cryptographic hash (such as SHA-256) and lock it.
2. Work Exclusively on Copies: Create a working duplicate. Search, highlight, filter, and parse within the working copy.
3. Record Collection Metadata: Always note who collected the record, from which device hostname, at what exact time, and under what specific time zone (e.g., UTC or IST).

The Safe Pause
Ananya poses a final critical scenario:
“If an unfamiliar instruction might delete data, what comes next?”
The learner answers thoughtfully:
“Pause, record what I see, and contact the mentor.”
Ananya nods approvingly:
“Correct. A safe pause is better than an irreversible guess.”
section1_theory.keyTakeaway: Never modify original evidence files—always work on copies. Record the source, collection time, and actions. A safe pause is always better than an irreversible guess.
section1_theory.cdacScenario: Mentor Ananya demonstrates evidence preservation on raw logs and guides the learner through the safe pause protocol.

section1_theory.title: The service we will follow
section1_theory.subtitle: The Recurring Finance Support Case & Entity Separation
section1_theory.content:
To make your learning realistic and consistent, our course does not present disconnected, random alert puzzles. Instead, we follow a single, coherent business environment across multiple releases of evidence.

Mentor Ananya displays a business overview card:
“Our recurring case follows account FIN-OPS-01 and workstation BLR-BR-WS-04; these are fictional learning identifiers.”
The learner asks for clarification:
“Is FIN-OPS-01 the computer's name?”
Ananya responds with an essential distinction:
“No. It is an account label. The workstation is a separate entity, and an account does not prove who was at the keyboard.”

The Four Distinct Entities in Security Telemetry
In security operations, confusion between devices, accounts, and human users causes catastrophic investigative errors. Ananya breaks down the four distinct entities you will track:
1. Business Service: The organizational process providing business value. Here, it is the fictional Branch Finance Support service, which handles staff portals, invoices, and shared branch documents.
2. User Account (FIN-OPS-01): A digital security credential used to log into systems and access services. An account is an identity token, not a physical box.
3. Workstation Endpoint (BLR-BR-WS-04): The physical computer hardware located on desk 4 at the Bengaluru branch. It has its own operating system and disk.
4. Network Address (10.10.20.15): The temporary IP address leased to the workstation by the branch DHCP router.

The Human Factor & Forensic Restraint
Ananya emphasizes:
“Which label identifies the workstation in our story?”
The learner replies:
“BLR-BR-WS-04.”
Ananya nods:
“Right. Keeping entities separate will prevent many investigation mistakes.”
If an alert states that account FIN-OPS-01 accessed a file at 02:00 AM, a disciplined analyst writes: “Activity was recorded under account FIN-OPS-01 from host BLR-BR-WS-04.” They do NOT jump to conclusions and accuse a specific employee of being awake and typing at that hour!
section1_theory.keyTakeaway: An account (FIN-OPS-01) is not a workstation (BLR-BR-WS-04), and an account name does not prove who was physically at the keyboard. Keeping entities separate prevents fundamental investigation mistakes.

Any physical or virtual computing device (workstation, server, mobile device) connected to the organizational network infrastructure.

section1_theory.title: The route from beginner to L1
section1_theory.subtitle: The 4-Section Learning Architecture & Your Path to Supervised L1 Readiness
section1_theory.content:
Mentor Ananya brings up the grand roadmap of the entire curriculum. A pathway lights up across 15 modules:
Computers (M01) ➔ Networks (M02) ➔ Security Fundamentals (M03) ➔ Alert Triage (M04) ➔ SIEM Search (M05) ➔ Log Analysis (M06) ➔ Host & Network Monitoring (M07–M08) ➔ EDR & Ecosystems (M09–M10) ➔ Identity & Threat Intel (M11) ➔ Automation & ATT&CK (M12–M13) ➔ Incident Handover (M14).

Ananya describes the consistent structure of your daily shifts:
“Each chapter gives you theory, a visual or demonstration, an activity, and a short knowledge check.”
The learner asks:
“When will I work without you explaining every click?”
Ananya explains how scaffolding works:
“Support gradually reduces. By the final simulation, you will triage, document, and escalate within an L1 playbook.”

The 4-Section Learning Engine
Every chapter in this course follows an active, predictable 4-section rhythm:
1. Section 1: Theory Briefing — Opening mentor dialogue, clear everyday analogies, plain-English mechanisms, and formal NIST/ISO definitions.
2. Section 2: Animated Visual Story — Vector simulations illustrating system mechanics with strict, concise labels so you can watch telemetry in motion.
3. Section 3: Interactive Activity — Hands-on sandboxes where you sort evidence, match concepts, or trace packet routes without fear of making mistakes.
4. Section 4: Knowledge Check — Scenario-based questions that validate your retention and build analytical muscle memory.

Setting Clear Expectations
Ananya concludes with an essential question regarding your destination:
“Does finishing this course automatically authorise production access or award an external certification?”
The learner replies accurately:
“No. It develops foundational skills; workplace authorisation and certification are separate.”
Ananya smiles:
“Exactly. Your destination is evidence-based beginner L1 practice, not instant expertise.”
section1_theory.keyTakeaway: The learning journey moves through 4 consistent sections per chapter with scaffolded support that gradually reduces. Your destination is evidence-based beginner L1 practice.
section1_theory.cdacScenario: Mentor Ananya outlines the 15-module learning roadmap and explains the 4-section chapter model leading to supervised L1 practice.

section1_theory.title: Hardware, OS and accounts
section1_theory.subtitle: A Computer Becomes Understandable: Physical Components, The Operating System & Account Boundaries
section1_theory.content:
Mentor Ravi sits beside you at the branch finance desk. On the screen, an animated diagram illuminates the internal workings of workstation BLR-BR-WS-04 without taking any physical screws out of the machine.

Ravi begins with a reassuring smile:
“Think of the computer as cooperating parts: processor, memory, storage, and devices for input and output.”
The learner asks a natural question:
“Are memory and storage the same thing?”
Ravi shakes his head gently:
“Memory supports current work; storage keeps files beyond a restart. The operating system coordinates resources and access.”

1. Familiar Situation: Working at an Office Desk
Imagine you are sitting at a branch desk creating a monthly budget spreadsheet. You type numbers on the keyboard, watch them appear on the screen, calculate a total, and save the document before shutting down for the night. You don't need to know electronic circuit design to notice that the computer does three different jobs: it processes numbers, it holds your active window open, and it files the spreadsheet away permanently.

2. Plain-Language Explanation: The Four Cooperating Parts
Every computer relies on four fundamental elements:
• Processor (CPU): The electronic engine that performs calculations and follows software instructions billions of times each second.
• Volatile Memory (RAM): The fast temporary workspace. When you open an application or document, it loads into RAM so the CPU can read it instantly. When power is turned off, everything in RAM evaporates.
• Persistent Storage (SSD or HDD): The permanent digital filing cabinet. Your operating system, spreadsheets, and emails remain safely saved here even when the machine is shut down.
• Input & Output (I/O): Keyboards and mice bring your commands in; monitors and network cards send information out.

3. The Operating System: The Master Coordinator
Raw silicon chips cannot run applications on their own. The Operating System (such as Microsoft Windows or Linux) is the master coordinator. The inner core of the OS—the Kernel—manages physical hardware drivers, divides CPU time between programs, and isolates memory so one frozen application cannot crash the whole machine.

4. User Accounts & Least Privilege
The OS creates User Accounts to establish identity and security boundaries:
• Standard User Account: Used for everyday work (typing documents, browsing, reviewing invoices). Standard users can save their own files but cannot modify operating system files or install device drivers.
• Administrator / Root Account: Holds master system authority to change system settings, install software, and reconfigure security policies.
The Principle of Least Privilege (PoLP) requires that users operate with the minimum permissions needed for their daily tasks. If an employee with a standard account opens a malicious attachment by mistake, the damage is contained within their personal workspace—the malware cannot silently overwrite core system files.

5. Story Example: Workstation BLR-BR-WS-04
At our CDAC Bengaluru branch finance desk, account FIN-OPS-01 logs into workstation BLR-BR-WS-04. Ravi shows how opening an invoice report loads data from the SSD into RAM, where the CPU calculates totals. Because FIN-OPS-01 is a standard user, the operating system prevents any accidental or malicious changes to protected Windows system directories.

Ravi checks your understanding:
“Which usually retains a saved report after the power is turned off?”
The learner responds:
“Storage.”
Ravi nods:
“Correct. You now have a simple model for understanding what a workstation does.”
section1_theory.keyTakeaway: A computer consists of cooperating parts: processor (CPU), temporary working memory (RAM), persistent storage (SSD/HDD), and the operating system that coordinates them. User accounts enforce least privilege to contain potential harm.

section1_theory.title: Files, paths and permissions
section1_theory.subtitle: Who Can Open This Folder? File Paths, Access Control & Temporary Staging Directories
section1_theory.content:
Mentor Ravi brings up a folder view on workstation BLR-BR-WS-04. Two user sessions are displayed side by side: one account opens a finance report with ease, while a second account clicks the exact same folder and receives an “Access Denied” dialog.

Ravi explains the core principle:
“A path locates a file. Permissions describe what an account is allowed to do with it.”
The learner glances at a folder labeled Temp and asks:
“If a file is in a temporary folder, does that make it malicious?”
Ravi smiles warmly:
“No. Temporary folders have legitimate uses, but writable locations can matter when we investigate suspicious execution.”

1. Familiar Situation: Shared Office Folders & Locked Cabinets
In any busy office, some documents are open for all staff to read (like cafeteria menus or company holiday lists), while payroll records and personnel evaluations are locked in human resources filing cabinets. If you don't have the key, the drawer stays locked. The computer enforces the exact same rules digitally.

2. Plain-Language Explanation: Paths & Permissions
• File & Folder: A file is a named collection of data (like a document, image, or script); a folder (directory) organizes files into logical groups.
• Path: The full digital address specifying where a file lives. In Windows, paths start with a drive letter (such as C:\Finance\Reports\july.xlsx). In Linux, paths start from the root forward slash (such as /var/log/syslog).
• Permissions: The rules governing actions on a file:
  - Read (R): View or open the contents.
  - Write (W): Modify, overwrite, or delete the file.
  - Execute (X): Run the file as an active software program or script.

3. Access Denied: A Security Boundary, Not a Malfunction
When an operating system displays “Access Denied”, beginner users often worry that the computer crashed or the hard drive is corrupted. Ravi poses a key question:
“Does an access-denied message mean the computer is broken?”
The learner answers thoughtfully:
“Not necessarily; the account may lack permission.”
Ravi confirms:
“Exactly. Record the account, path, requested action, and result before drawing conclusions.”

4. Why Writable Locations Matter in Security Triage
Standard enterprise users are forbidden from writing files to system directories like C:\Windows\System32 or /etc. However, users must be able to create scratch files, so operating systems provide user-writable temporary directories—such as %TEMP% (C:\Users\<User>\AppData\Local\Temp) in Windows or /tmp in Linux.
Because standard users have write access here, software installers unpack setup files into Temp. Adversaries exploit this same permission to drop unauthorized executables without needing administrative rights. A file in Temp is not automatically malware, but an executable launching from Temp is a clue that warrants immediate investigation.

5. Story Example: Investigating BLR-BR-WS-04
On workstation BLR-BR-WS-04, user account FIN-OPS-01 accesses the shared folder C:\Finance\Invoices. The account possesses Read and Write permissions for daily invoices. However, when an unverified script attempts to write an executable into C:\Windows\System32, Windows halts the operation with an Access Denied error. Ravi notes: the defense worked as designed; our job as analysts is to record what happened factually.
section1_theory.keyTakeaway: A file path provides its precise digital address, while permissions determine which accounts can Read, Write, or Execute it. An access-denied message is an intentional security boundary, not a system failure. Always verify path context.
section1_theory.cdacScenario: Ravi demonstrates file paths, NTFS access permissions, and temporary directory behavior on BLR-BR-WS-04, showing why access-denied errors protect system integrity.

questions.question: During an alert review on host BLR-BR-WS-04, an analyst discovers an executable file located in C:\Users\FIN-OPS-01\AppData\Local\Temp\. What is the most accurate assessment of this file location?
options: Every file located in a temporary directory is guaranteed to be hostile malware
Temporary folders have legitimate uses, but user-writable paths warrant verification because droppers often stage files there without admin rights
Windows automatically prohibits all software from ever running in temporary directories
Files in temporary directories can only be created by system administrators
questions.explanation: Temporary folders are world-writable by the user session. Many legitimate installers use them, but adversaries also leverage them. The location requires careful context, not automatic assumption.

questions.question:
Review the following workstation access control configuration:
Path: C:\BranchFinance\AuditReports\
Account: FIN-OPS-01 | Rights: Read, ListDirectory
Account: Local_Admin | Rights: Full Control
If user FIN-OPS-01 attempts to modify and overwrite an existing report in this folder, what will occur?
options: The report will be successfully overwritten because the user has Read access
The operating system will block the change with an access error because the account lacks Write permission
The operating system will automatically promote FIN-OPS-01 to administrator status
The file will be permanently deleted from the hard drive
questions.explanation: Permissions are granular. Having Read and List permissions does not grant Write or Modify permissions. The operating system will block the modification attempt.

questions.question: An apprentice analyst triaging BLR-BR-WS-04 notices that an unapproved executable attempted to write to C:\Program Files\ under account FIN-OPS-01 and failed due to insufficient privileges. What is the most disciplined next step?
options: Grant account FIN-OPS-01 permanent local administrator rights so the program can complete its task
Record the account, full path, attempted action, and failure outcome, then check whether the execution was part of an approved software deployment
Immediately format the hard drive of BLR-BR-WS-04 without recording notes
Delete the user account FIN-OPS-01 from the domain controller
questions.explanation: Disciplined analysts record observable facts (account, path, action, outcome) and verify whether the action was scheduled business maintenance before jumping to drastic, unsupported conclusions.

section1_theory.title: What processes and services do
section1_theory.subtitle: Programs Doing Work: Process Instances, Process IDs (PIDs) & Background Services
section1_theory.content:
Mentor Ravi gestures to the clean desktop of workstation BLR-BR-WS-04. With a double-click, he opens a simple text editor. A plain white window appears on the screen.

Ravi explains the distinction:
“A program is stored instructions; a process is a running instance. Services often perform background work.”
The learner watches the window appear and asks:
“So every process belongs to a window I can see?”
Ravi shakes his head:
“No. Many do not. Processes have identifiers, accounts, executable paths, and sometimes parent processes.”

1. Familiar Situation: Recipes vs Active Cooking
Think of a recipe in a printed cookbook. Sitting on the kitchen shelf, the recipe is just text on paper—it isn't baking a cake or slicing vegetables. But when a chef steps up to the counter and begins following the steps, an active cooking session begins. If two chefs follow the same recipe at two different counters at the same time, you have two independent cooking sessions running simultaneously.

2. Plain-Language Explanation: Programs vs Processes
• Program: The compiled code and instructions stored permanently on disk (for example, notepad.exe stored in C:\Windows\System32).
• Process: An active, running instance of that program loaded into memory (RAM) and executing on the processor (CPU).
• Process Identifier (PID): A unique temporary number assigned by the operating system to identify each running process.
Ravi demonstrates by opening a second copy of the text editor. Both windows say “Notepad”, but when Ravi checks the task list, one is PID 4120 and the other is PID 6844.

Ravi tests your reasoning:
“If the editor starts twice, must both instances have the same process identifier?”
The learner replies:
“No; each running instance can have its own identifier.”
Ravi confirms:
“Correct. A process name alone is not a unique identity.”

3. Parent-Child Process Lineage (PPID)
Processes rarely start by magic; almost every process is launched by another process. The creator is the Parent Process, and the newly launched task is the Child Process.
• Normal Example: You open your desktop folder and double-click an invoice. The desktop shell (explorer.exe) is the parent, and the spreadsheet app (excel.exe) is the child.
• Suspicious Example: A word document (winword.exe) suddenly launches a script interpreter (powershell.exe) in the background. Tracking the Parent Process ID (PPID) helps analysts immediately spot unauthorized command execution.

4. Background Services: Invisible Helpers
Many crucial operating system tasks run silently in the background without any visible desktop window, menu bar, or taskbar icon. These are called Services (in Windows) or Daemons (in Linux). For example, the print spooler service waits quietly for documents to print, and the time synchronization service keeps the system clock accurate. They start when the computer boots and run under dedicated system accounts.

5. Story Example: Observing BLR-BR-WS-04
On workstation BLR-BR-WS-04, Ravi guides you to inspect the active task list. You identify account FIN-OPS-01 running an accounting tool under PID 3312, spawned by explorer.exe. Meanwhile, in the background, the Windows Service Host (svchost.exe) runs under PID 916 with no visible desktop window, faithfully serving background network requests.
section1_theory.keyTakeaway: A program is stored code on disk; a process is an active instance running in memory with its own Process ID (PID). Services perform necessary background work without desktop windows. Tracing parent-child relationships reveals how tasks originated.

section1_theory.title: Routine versus unfamiliar activity
section1_theory.subtitle: Unfamiliar Does Not Mean Hostile: Baselining, Context Verification & Masquerading Detection
section1_theory.content:
Mentor Ravi displays two process cards side by side on his screen. One card shows an unfamiliar software updater from a hardware vendor; the other shows an executable whose name closely mimics a core Windows service.

Ravi explains the core analytical principle:
“We investigate context: path, publisher information, account, parent process, time, and approved activity.”
The learner looks at the second card and remarks:
“This name resembles a Windows component. Is that enough to trust it?”
Ravi shakes his head firmly:
“No. Names can be misleading. Neither a familiar name nor a strange name settles the question.”

1. Familiar Situation: Odd Names in the Task Manager
Have you ever opened your computer's task manager and felt alarmed by strange process names like ctfmon.exe, spoolsv.exe, or igfxpers.exe? To someone without an IT background, these look like secret codes or dangerous viruses. In reality, they are standard system components that help manage keyboards, printers, and graphics cards.

2. Plain-Language Explanation: Routine vs Unfamiliar
Every organization develops an Operational Baseline—a picture of what normal daily computer activity looks like:
• Routine Activity: Everyday business tools (office software, approved branch banking portals, standard backup scripts) executing from standard directories at expected working hours.
• Unfamiliar Activity: An executable name or background task you haven't seen before. Unfamiliar does NOT automatically mean malicious! It could be a scheduled software update, a newly deployed accounting patch, or a printer driver.
Disciplined analysts do not raise emergency panic alarms just because a filename looks strange. They investigate its context.

3. The Danger of Masquerading (Typosquatting)
Because attackers know analysts look for obvious malware names, they frequently use Masquerading. They name their malicious files to look almost identical to trusted system files:
• Authentic Windows Service Host: svchost.exe (spelled with the letter 'o', located strictly in C:\Windows\System32, signed by Microsoft).
• Typosquatted Imposter: svch0st.exe (substituting the digit '0' for the letter 'o', located in C:\Users\Public\ or C:\Temp\, unsigned).

Ravi points to the suspicious card and asks:
“You see svch0st.exe, with a zero. What can you responsibly say?”
The learner replies with disciplined accuracy:
“The name is suspiciously similar; I should verify its path and other evidence.”
Ravi beams with approval:
“Good. You have identified a reason to investigate without claiming proof of malware.”

4. The 5-Point Context Checklist
When evaluating an unfamiliar process, verify these five contextual pillars:
1. Directory Path: Does it run from C:\Program Files\ or System32, or from a temporary user-writable folder?
2. Digital Publisher: Is the file digitally signed by a trusted vendor (like Microsoft or your branch software supplier)?
3. User Account: Is it running under a system service account or an interactive standard user?
4. Parent Process: Did an authorized system service launch it, or was it spawned by a suspicious command script?
5. Approved Change Window: Did IT schedule maintenance or an update at this specific hour?

5. Story Example: Triage on BLR-BR-WS-04
At the Bengaluru branch, an automated alert flags an unfamiliar process named branch_sync.exe. An apprentice analyst might want to immediately kill the process and unplug the cable. Mentor Ravi pauses and checks the context: the binary lives in C:\Program Files\BranchTools\, is signed by the CDAC banking portal vendor, and corresponds to an approved 14:00 branch sync schedule. The activity is routine and benign. Fact-based verification prevented a disruptive false alarm!
section1_theory.keyTakeaway: Unfamiliar does not mean hostile, and a familiar name does not guarantee safety. Never judge an executable by filename alone; always verify directory path, parent process, digital signature, and approved business context.

Ignore the executable completely because any file ending in .exe is safe

Record 1: Name: svchost.exe | Path: C:\Windows\System32\svchost.exe | Parent: services.exe | Signed: Microsoft Corporation
Record 2: Name: svch0st.exe | Path: C:\Users\FIN-OPS-01\AppData\Local\Temp\svch0st.exe | Parent: cmd.exe | Signed: Unsigned
Why does Record 2 represent a significant reason to investigate?
options: Because Record 2 runs from System32
Because Record 2 is signed by Microsoft Corporation
Because Record 2 uses typosquatting (digit 0 instead of letter o), executes from a user temporary directory, and was spawned by a command shell
Because Record 2 has a lower Process ID than Record 1

questions.explanation: Office productivity applications do not legitimately spawn PowerShell to run encoded commands. Documenting the specific parent-child lineage and escalating follows disciplined L1 triage.

section1_theory.title: Command-line essentials
section1_theory.subtitle: Talking to the Workstation: Safe Observational Commands, Question-First Triage & Avoiding Destructive Actions
section1_theory.content:
Mentor Ravi opens a black terminal window on workstation BLR-BR-WS-04. A simple white prompt blinks patiently on the screen: C:\Users\FIN-OPS-01>. Beside the monitor, Ravi places three clear index cards: “Which device?”, “Who am I?”, and “What is running?”.

Ravi introduces the interface:
“A command line is another interface. We will use only approved observational commands in this lab.”
The learner looks at the blank screen with slight hesitation:
“Do I need to memorise every command?”
Ravi reassures them with a smile:
“No. Learn the question first; use a reference sheet and understand the output before continuing.”

1. Familiar Situation: Speaking Directly to a Helpful Assistant
If you ask a store assistant, “Excuse me, which aisle has printer paper?”, they give you a direct, specific answer. The command line works the same way: instead of navigating five graphical menus and searching for icons with a mouse, you type a short question into the terminal, press Enter, and the operating system replies immediately with the exact facts.

2. The Question-First Approach to CLI
Beginners often feel overwhelmed by thousands of technical command options. Professional analysts never memorize everything; they approach the terminal with a specific investigation question:
• Question 1: “Which computer is this?” ➔ Run: hostname
  Output: BLR-BR-WS-04 (identifies the physical branch machine).
• Question 2: “Which account is active in this session?” ➔ Run: whoami
  Output: cdac\fin-ops-01 (identifies the user account and domain).
• Question 3: “What programs are currently active in memory?” ➔ Run: tasklist
  Output: A structured table showing image names, PIDs, session names, and memory usage.

3. The Golden Rule of Live Triage: Observational vs Destructive Commands
In security triage, our goal is to observe and preserve evidence without altering system state.
• Safe Observational Commands: Commands like hostname, whoami, tasklist, and netstat only read information from memory. They do not delete files, terminate services, or modify configurations.
• Risky / Destructive Commands: Commands like del, rm, format, or taskkill /f change or destroy data.
Ravi asks an essential safety question:
“If a command asks you to delete files, is it part of today's observation exercise?”
The learner answers firmly:
“No. I should stop and check the instructions.”
Ravi nods with satisfaction:
“Correct. Copying unfamiliar commands blindly is not an analyst skill.”

4. Understanding Output Before Moving On
Running a command is only half the job; an analyst must understand what the terminal returns. If you run whoami /user, the output displays the account name and a long string called a Security Identifier (SID) like S-1-5-21-.... This SID is the machine's internal badge number for that account. Take a moment to read the columns and numbers rather than rushing to type the next command.

5. Story Example: Lab Triage on BLR-BR-WS-04
Inside the isolated training VM at CDAC Bengaluru, the learner follows Ravi's instructions:
1. Types hostname ➔ Terminal returns BLR-BR-WS-04.
2. Types whoami ➔ Terminal returns cdac\FIN-OPS-01.
3. Types tasklist ➔ Identifies the active accounting software process.
The learner records these three verified facts into an initial observation card. Not a single file was altered, and valuable evidence was safely documented!
section1_theory.keyTakeaway: The command-line is an interface for asking questions. Learn the question before the command, rely on reference sheets, use approved observational commands (hostname, whoami, tasklist), and never copy or execute destructive commands blindly.

section1_theory.title: Users, hostnames and timestamps
section1_theory.subtitle: An Identity Card for Evidence: Disambiguating Entities, Preserving Time Zones & Professional Triage Documentation
section1_theory.content:
Mentor Ravi places an initial scrap of paper on the desk. Written in scribbled pencil is an ambiguous note from a previous shift: “Someone did something yesterday on the finance PC.”

Ravi shakes his head with a gentle grin:
“These fields give observations an address in the investigation: which system, which account, and when.”
The learner points to the account field and asks:
“If the account is FIN-OPS-01, can I write that the employee personally performed every action?”
Ravi provides an essential forensic guideline:
“Not from that field alone. Say the activity was recorded under that account.”

1. Familiar Situation: A Lost Package Without an Address
Imagine receiving an urgent postal delivery with no sender name, no street address, and no postal date stamp—just a note saying “Important item enclosed.” You would have no idea who sent it, which house it belongs to, or whether it arrived today or three weeks ago. Digital evidence without an address is equally useless in a security investigation.

2. The 3-Part Workstation Evidence Identity Card
To give any security observation a solid, indisputable address, an analyst documents three fundamental anchor fields:
• 1. Hostname (Which computer?): The unique machine name on the enterprise network (e.g., BLR-BR-WS-04). This separates the hardware asset from other laptops and servers.
• 2. Account Identifier (Under which identity?): The credential logged into the session (e.g., FIN-OPS-01). Remember: an account is an identity token, not proof of who sat in the chair! Credentials can be shared, automated, or compromised. Always write: “Activity recorded under account FIN-OPS-01”.
• 3. Timestamp & Explicit Time Zone (When did it occur?): The exact hour, minute, second, and time zone offset (e.g., 2026-10-14 14:30:00 IST [+05:30]).

3. Why Time Zones Matter: The UTC Standard
Ravi tests your reasoning on timestamps:
“Why preserve the time zone as well as the clock time?”
The learner answers thoughtfully:
“Because the same clock reading can mean different moments in different zones.”
Ravi confirms:
“Exactly. Your first useful evidence note is now clear enough for someone else to read.”
CDAC Bengaluru operates in Indian Standard Time (IST, UTC+05:30). If an event happens at 14:30:00 IST and you omit the time zone, an analyst in London (UTC) reading “14:30” would assume the event happened five and a half hours later! Security Operations Centres standardize on Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) to sequence events across global sensors accurately:
14:30:00 IST minus 05:30:00 = 09:00:00 UTC.

4. Repairing Vague Notes into Professional Triage Artifacts
Compare these two case notes:
• Vague & Unusable: “Finance user had a virus yesterday.” (Who? Which PC? When? What virus?)
• Professional & Verifiable: “Host: BLR-BR-WS-04 | Account: FIN-OPS-01 | Time: 2026-10-14 14:30:12 IST (09:00:12 UTC) | Observable: Execution of unapproved script blocked in %TEMP% by endpoint policy.”

5. Story Example: Completing the Case Note on BLR-BR-WS-04
Beside Mentor Ravi, the learner completes their first official workstation observation card for the recurring branch finance case. The card records:
• Machine: BLR-BR-WS-04
• Account: FIN-OPS-01
• Timestamp: 2026-10-14 14:30:00 IST (UTC+05:30) / 09:00:00 UTC
• Action: Safe baseline verification complete; standard user session active; no elevated administrative anomalies detected.
Ravi signs off on the note with an encouraging nod: you have completed Module 01 and learned to observe, document, and reason like a true L1 apprentice!
section1_theory.keyTakeaway: Every piece of evidence requires an address: Hostname, Account, and exact Timestamp with an explicit time zone. Never confuse an account with proof of a person. Standardizing timestamps to UTC ensures accurate chronological timelines.

options: It proves that employee Ramesh was physically sitting at the keyboard typing

It proves that the computer has been compromised by malware
questions.explanation: An account identifier is a digital credential context. It verifies which account token is active, not which human being was physically touching the keys.

questions.question: Why must a security analyst always include the explicit time zone (such as IST / UTC+05:30 or UTC) when recording an event timestamp in an incident note?
options: Because computers in different countries cannot subtract numbers
Because omitting the time zone causes cross-region event logs to be misaligned or sequenced in the wrong chronological order
Because recording the time zone makes log files smaller on disk
Because time zones prevent antivirus software from alerting
questions.explanation: Sensors and analysts operate across distributed geographic regions. Without an explicit time zone or UTC normalization, reconstructing the true order of events across firewalls and endpoints is impossible.

questions.explanation: A professional triage note records specific, verifiable observables (host, account, normalized time, method) without speculation or accusatory language.

options: Run `del C:\*.*` across the network to wipe potential infections immediately

Close the ticket as resolved because vague tickets are unimportant
questions.explanation: Disciplined analysts do not guess or execute destructive commands. They use non-invasive observational queries and reference sheets to identify the specific host, account, and timestamp.

terminologyScaffolding.analogy: Like a sports team's scouting playbook: studying the opposing team's preferred formations, trick plays, and quarterback tendencies so defenders can anticipate and block the play before the ball is thrown.
terminologyScaffolding.definition: An evidence-based knowledge repository and matrix of adversary tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) used to understand threat actor methods and identify gaps in defensive coverage.
terminologyScaffolding.whyItMatters: Transforms defense from reactive guessing to proactive hunting by mapping observable artifacts directly to documented adversary behaviors.

instructionalContext.conceptHeadline: Instructional Foundations: Threat Intelligence & MITRE ATT&CK Mapping
instructionalContext.overview: In this chapter, analysts focus on the core principles of Assets, threats and vulnerabilities. Grounded in active CDAC Bengaluru SOC protocols, you will learn to understand the foundational mechanics of threat intelligence & mitre att&ck mapping, identify key observables, and apply empirical triage discipline.

processStages.explanation: Inspect raw event streams from sensors to locate relevant assets, threats and vulnerabilities indicators and extract core observables (User, Host, IP).
Compare observed activity against organizational baselines, change management records, and standard operating procedures.
Document findings clearly with UTC timestamps, rule out benign false positives, and formulate the appropriate tier-1 response.

terminologyScaffolding.definition: A structured operational methodology and telemetry verification protocol governing how enrichment and notification use cases is detected, analyzed, and mitigated within enterprise SOC workflows.
terminologyScaffolding.whyItMatters: Ensures L1 analysts can rapidly isolate genuine security threats, eliminate noisy false alarms, and maintain continuous visibility across organizational assets.

instructionalContext.conceptHeadline: Instructional Foundations: Enrichment and notification use cases
instructionalContext.overview: In this chapter, analysts focus on the core principles of Enrichment and notification use cases. Grounded in active CDAC Bengaluru SOC protocols, you will learn to understand the foundational mechanics of enrichment and notification use cases, identify key observables, and apply empirical triage discipline.

processStages.explanation: Inspect raw event streams from sensors to locate relevant enrichment and notification use cases indicators and extract core observables (User, Host, IP).
Compare observed activity against organizational baselines, change management records, and standard operating procedures.
Document findings clearly with UTC timestamps, rule out benign false positives, and formulate the appropriate tier-1 response.
